source_row.description: This research focused on the use of information sources about the organizational environment by startup managers. It sought to characterize the relevance of sectors within the external environment to the business, the factors that motivate managers to seek information, and the degree of relevance and reliability of the information sources. The research methodology was based on a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods. For quantitative data collection, an online questionnaire was used, obtaining 60 responses. After analyzing the results, as a qualitative research method, interviews were conducted with three managers involved in incubation, acceleration, and investment programs for startups, so that the data could be discussed. The results demonstrated that entrepreneurs recognize customers and technology as the main sectors of the external environment affecting their businesses, and that there is a concern in seeking information to generate innovations and support decisions. Furthermore, it was possible to verify the relevance and reliability attributed to internal information sources, such as partners/employees and databases from their own companies, and the relevance of new digital information sources, to the detriment of traditional sources.
source_row.title: Use of information sources by startup managers

records.title: Use of information sources by startup managers

source_row.description: Classic decision theory requires that rational agents show description invariance: which description is chosen should not matter for judgments, preferences, or choices given the descriptions are co-extensive. Framing research has amply demonstrated a failure of description invariance by showing that the choice of the description has a systematic effect on judgments, preferences, and choices. Specifically, framing research has shown that linguistically different descriptions of seemingly equivalent options frequently lead to preference reversals.
source_row.title: A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects

source_row.description: The text uses the metaphor of three baseball umpires to discuss the illusion of impartiality in judgments. While one recognizes his human limitations, the others assume infallibility. From this, the article shows that judges, like any person, are also subject to heuristics and cognitive biases, which function as mental shortcuts to save resources, but can generate systematic errors in decisions. These biases influence everything from the analysis of evidence to sentencing, revealing that, despite experience and training, irrelevant factors can predictably distort judgments, casting doubt on the idea of total objectivity in the judicial process.

source_row.description: This article discusses potential pitfalls that can arise from data-driven decision making when not properly balanced with human judgment, strategic thinking, and organizational context. Drawing on the author's experience as a management consultant, key risks are examined such as the "tyranny of metrics" when KPIs distort goals, misinterpreting correlations as causation, overgeneralizing from limited data sets, confirmation bias within "filter bubbles," and overemphasizing quantitative data at the expense of human elements. Specific industry examples are provided to illustrate unintended consequences that have occurred. The article advocates for maintaining a multidisciplinary, questioning approach to analytics, constantly reevaluating metrics and models, supplementing internal data with external realities, and blending quantitative and qualitative inputs. Balancing these risks and enacting various safeguards can maximize the benefits of fact-based management while avoiding potential downsides.
source_row.title: When Analysis Outruns Wisdom: Potential Pitfalls of Data-Driven Decision-Making

source_row.description: This paper examines how organizations make decisions under uncertainty and highlights the role of governance in managing risk-taking. It presents a structured framework for decision-making that integrates tools such as scenario analysis, decision trees, and probabilistic simulations to evaluate potential outcomes and downside risks.The key takeaway is that high-quality decisions are not defined by outcomes alone, but by the robustness of the process—particularly the explicit consideration of multiple scenarios, assumptions, and risk exposures. By formalizing this process, organizations enhance transparency, improve accountability, and strengthen the defensibility of executive decisions before boards and stakeholders.
source_row.title: Risk Taking: A Corporate Governance Perspective

records.title: Risk Taking: A Corporate Governance Perspective

source_row.description: This article explores how organizations can enhance decision-making by integrating strategic intelligence into enterprise risk management (ERM). It emphasizes the importance of moving beyond traditional, compliance-driven risk frameworks toward a more forward-looking approach that incorporates scenario planning, stress testing, and continuous monitoring of external signals.The core idea is that organizations should actively test strategic assumptions under different scenarios, enabling leaders to anticipate potential disruptions and respond proactively. By doing so, management teams can make more resilient decisions under uncertainty, while boards gain greater visibility into key risks, underlying assumptions, and preparedness for adverse outcomes.Ultimately, the integration of strategic intelligence into ERM strengthens governance, improves the quality of strategic discussions at the board level, and supports more informed, transparent, and defensible executive decision-making.
source_row.title: Strategic Intelligence: An Integrated Approach to Enterprise Risk Management
